prompt: Which kind of lock-in is the only one with a date written on it?
hint: Finance will remind you of it.

choices.text: Data stored in Cloud Storage
choices.why: Data grows heavier month by month, but no contract ends.

choices.text: Calls to the Pub/Sub API
choices.why: An API ties you by code, not by a term.

choices.text: A committed use discount
choices.why: Right. One or three years, used or not.

choices.text: IAM roles and service accounts
choices.why: Permissions tie you by design, with no end date.

prompt: Why does the lesson call permissions the part of a migration that fails quietly?
hint: What happens when a service starts?

choices.text: A service starts fine and then cannot read what it needs
choices.why: Right. Nothing fails at deploy; the failure waits for the first read.

choices.text: IAM roles cannot be exported from Google Cloud
choices.why: They can be listed; the trouble is that other providers model them differently.

choices.text: Permissions are billed per role and the bill arrives late
choices.why: IAM itself is not billed per role.

choices.text: Other providers have no notion of a service identity at all
choices.why: They do, under other names and rules.

prompt: Match each kind of lock-in to what undoing it costs.
hint: The table at the end of the section.

pairs.right: Egress, copy time and a cutover
The months left on the term

prompt: A team refuses Pub/Sub "to avoid lock-in" and builds its own queue on a machine. By the section's argument, what did it trade?
hint: Every kind of lock-in is also a kind of value.

choices.text: Nothing: a queue on a machine is portable and equally reliable
choices.why: It is portable; whether it is as reliable is the work they just took on.

choices.text: Data gravity, because the queue now holds the data
choices.why: A queue on their own machine is still in Google Cloud; nothing moved.

choices.text: A commitment, since a machine must be reserved for a year
choices.why: Machines need no commitment; that is optional.

choices.text: A ready service, for a rewrite nobody has asked for
choices.why: Right. The question is which lock-in buys enough; this one bought a lot.

prompt: Data is the heaviest thing a system owns, and services tend to settle near it: the lesson calls this data ___.
hint: A word from physics.

prompt: Which seam does the lesson call the strongest on its list?
hint: It runs unchanged on every provider's container service.

choices.text: Terraform
choices.why: Terraform is a workflow seam; its resources do not move.

choices.text: The OCI container image
choices.why: Right. The same image runs on Cloud Run, any Kubernetes and Docker.

choices.text: The Pub/Sub client library
choices.why: Pub/Sub has no other implementation; it is the opposite of a seam.

choices.text: A Cloud Run revision tag
choices.why: Revision tags are platform configuration, written in Google's terms.

prompt: The status function answered on the laptop with "Server: gunicorn". What does that show?
hint: What is underneath the framework?

choices.text: That the function was proxied to Google and back
choices.why: The lab has no network; nothing left the laptop.

choices.text: That Cloud Run functions are deprecated in favour of gunicorn
choices.why: Nothing is deprecated; gunicorn is how the framework serves.

choices.text: A thin layer over a common Python web server
choices.why: Right. Nothing in it needs Google to run.

choices.text: That the decorator was ignored and Flask answered directly
choices.why: The decorator registered the function that answered.

prompt: The lesson advises putting every Pub/Sub call behind one module of the shop's own. What must that module not become?
hint: Think of the lowest common denominator.

choices.text: A framework flattening every provider to the weakest common features
choices.why: Right. That costs the features you chose Google for and leaves the data behind.

choices.text: A module with a name about the shop rather than about Google
choices.why: That naming is exactly what the lesson asks for.

choices.text: A short list of the places the shop touches Google
choices.why: That is what it should be.

choices.text: Code that the tests can replace with a fake
choices.why: A module that is easy to fake is a bonus, not a danger.

prompt: Cloud Run's service description follows the format of ___ Serving, which runs on any Kubernetes cluster that has it.
hint: Its apiVersion is serving.<name>.dev/v1.

prompt: Which of these are seams in the lesson's sense? Choose all that apply.
hint: An interface somebody else also implements.

choices.text: The CloudEvents envelope
choices.why: Right. A CNCF specification with libraries everywhere.

choices.text: The Functions Framework
choices.why: Right. Open source, and it ran on the laptop.

choices.text: A google_cloud_run_v2_service block
choices.why: It has no equivalent outside Google.

choices.text: The Firestore client library
choices.why: Firestore has no other implementation.

choices.text: The contract of listening on $PORT
choices.why: Right. Any container platform can honour it.

prompt: A handler reads Eventarc's CloudEvents. The shop moves to another provider whose router also emits CloudEvents. What still has to change?
hint: The envelope is shared; is the content?

choices.text: Nothing: CloudEvents makes the handler fully portable
choices.why: The envelope is portable; the event's fields are the source's own.

choices.text: The language: CloudEvents only has a Python library
choices.why: It has libraries in every major language.

choices.text: The HTTP port, which CloudEvents fixes at 8080
choices.why: CloudEvents says nothing about ports.

choices.text: The code reading storage-specific fields
choices.why: Right. An object event carries Cloud Storage's fields, and another store has others.

prompt: Using the tiers of the lesson, what does 1 TiB (1,024 GiB) of egress cost in one month, in USD?
hint: The first GiB is free; the rest is at 0.12.

prompt: With the same tiers, what do 2 TiB (2,048 GiB) cost in one month, in USD?
Why does the lesson call egress the kind of lock-in that grows silently?
hint: What happens to the store each month?

choices.text: Google raises egress prices a little every month
choices.why: The prices did not move; the volume did.

choices.text: The shop stores more each month than it deletes
choices.why: Right. The price of leaving rises with the data, and no bill says so.

choices.text: Egress is billed only on the day you leave
choices.why: It is billed whenever data leaves, but the warning is in the volume.

choices.text: The free first GiB shrinks as data grows
choices.why: The free GiB is fixed per month.

prompt: Of the three parts of the cost of leaving, which ones have a price list?
hint: Two of them are paid in people's time.

choices.text: All three, on Google's pricing pages
choices.why: Rewriting and overlap are measured in weeks, not on a page.

choices.text: Rewriting, because it is billed per call site
choices.why: Nobody bills per call site; the count estimates the weeks.

choices.text: Only moving the data
choices.why: Right. Egress has tiers and a program; the rest is time.

choices.text: Running both, because overlap is a fixed fee
choices.why: Overlap is everything running twice, for as long as it lasts.

prompt: A shop's systems cost 3,500 USD a month and the migration overlap lasts three months. Using the lesson's rough rule, what is the duplicate infrastructure, in USD?
hint: The overlap costs as much as the systems for its duration.

prompt: Google announced in 2024 that it waives egress for customers moving all their data off Google Cloud. How does the lesson tell you to treat that?
hint: On application, under conditions.

choices.text: Read the current terms before counting on it
choices.why: Right. It is a possibility with conditions, not a line to delete from the estimate.

choices.text: As a reason to stop estimating egress at all
choices.why: A waiver with conditions does not remove the estimate; it may not apply.

choices.text: As automatic for anyone who closes a project
choices.why: It is on application, and for moving everything out.

choices.text: As covering partial moves of a single service
choices.why: The announcement is about moving all of the data.

prompt: According to the lesson, what separates lock-in by accident from lock-in on purpose?
hint: Not which services are used.

choices.text: Using only services that have open-source equivalents
choices.why: The lesson accepts proprietary services chosen knowingly.

choices.text: Whether a committed use discount was signed
choices.why: A commitment is one kind of lock-in, chosen or not.

choices.text: Whether the team runs everything on GKE
choices.why: Running on GKE is a choice like any other, with its own ties.

choices.text: Whether the choice and its reasons were written down
choices.why: Right. The record is what makes it a decision.

prompt: When does the lesson say a committed use discount is money saved rather than money promised?
hint: What would you run anyway?

choices.text: When it covers the capacity you expect to need next year
choices.why: That is the case it calls money promised.

choices.text: When it covers a baseline that has already run for a year
choices.why: Right. You would pay for it anyway, so the discount is pure saving.

choices.text: When it is for three years rather than one
choices.why: A longer term is a bigger discount and a bigger promise.

choices.text: When it is signed in the month before renewal
choices.why: The month before renewal is when to look again, not what makes it a saving.

prompt: Why does the record give Cloud Scheduler "never, probably" as its condition to look again?
hint: What would leaving it take?

choices.text: Cloud Scheduler has no price, so it never needs review
choices.why: It costs 0.10 per job per 31 days after three free jobs.

choices.text: Scheduler jobs are covered by the commitment on Cloud Run
choices.why: The commitment is for Cloud Run; it says nothing about the scheduler.

choices.text: Any scheduler calling a URL replaces it
choices.why: Right. A dependency that costs nothing to leave needs little watching.

choices.text: Google guarantees Cloud Scheduler will never change
choices.why: No such guarantee exists; the argument is the cost of leaving.

prompt: Put the columns of a dependency record in the order the lesson uses.
hint: From the thing to the trigger.
trap: The last column is the one most teams leave out, and the one that keeps the record honest.

prompt: A team ships source code to Cloud Run with a buildpack instead of building its own image, "because it is simpler". Which rule of thumb does that run against, and why?
hint: A container instead of a source upload.

choices.text: Prefer the free seam: an image of their own
choices.why: Right. Building the image is a small step that keeps the strongest seam in their hands.

choices.text: Commit only to what you would run anyway
choices.why: No commitment is involved.

choices.text: Keep the data where you can afford to move it
choices.why: No data moves here.

choices.text: Accept the proprietary service and wrap it in a module
choices.why: There is nothing to wrap; the question is who owns the image.

prompt: Using the lesson's tiers, 10 TiB (10,240 GiB) leave in one month. What does it cost, in USD?
Which kind of lock-in does the shop's Terraform represent, by this lesson?
hint: A workflow seam, not a resource seam.

choices.text: None: Terraform makes every resource portable
choices.why: The habit moves; google_* resources do not.

choices.text: Data gravity, since the state file is data
choices.why: The state file is small and moves freely; the resources are the tie.

choices.text: A commitment, since providers are pinned to 8.9.0
choices.why: A pinned version is a choice you can change in a line.

choices.text: Platform configuration written in Google's terms
choices.why: Right. Rewriting it is part of what leaving costs.
